## ABSTRACT

Microplastics (MPs), widespread emerging pollutants across the globe, impose serious threats

to ecosystems and human health. To fully unravel their complex environmental behaviors and

advance pollution governance, high-efficiency, high-precision monitoring techniques are urgently

required. Given the major analytical obstacles arising from faint optical signals and highly variable

morphologies of MPs in environmental matrices, this work introduces YOLO-MPs, a physics-

guided deep learning framework designed to rapidly and precisely quantify five common MPs types

(fibers, fragments, films, pellets and linear pieces) collected from surface water. By employing

dynamic feature perception and adaptive background suppression modules, this model significantly

overcame interference from environmental artifacts such as water stains and inorganic particles,

while improving the capture capability for small-sized and low-contrast MPs. The results of the

improved algorithm showed a mean average precision at IoU 0.5 (mAP@50) of 92.68% with an

improvement of 3.70%, a precision (P) of 93.01% with an improvement of 4.54%, and an inference

time of 1.28 s per image, which was 13.03 times faster than manual detection. Additionally, a

module was developed to calculate MPs particle size based on a pixel-to-physical size mapping

ratio. The integrated system was successfully applied to analyze MPs in surface water from

Qiantang River, China, providing rapid, efficient, accurate, and low-cost analysis to support source

analysis and mitigation of MPs pollution.

## Keywords: MPs, YOLO-MPs, Morphology Analysis, Quantification, Surface

1.Introduction 1

Microplastics (MPs) refer to synthetic polymer particles smaller than 5 mm, originating from 2

primary MPs, such as plastic microbeads in personal care products, tire wear particles, and synthetic 3

fibers, as well as secondary MPs formed by the fragmentation of larger plastic debris in the 4

environment (Wang et al., 2019). Global annual emissions of MPs between 2020 and 2025 are 5

estimated to range from 10 million to 40 million tonnes, and this amount could double by 2040 6

without effective intervention (Thompson et al., 2024). Owing to their widespread occurrence in 7

freshwater, marine systems, and soils, MPs have raised increasing ecological and public health 8

concerns. They can cause physical damage and chemical toxicity to aquatic organisms (De-la-Torre, 9

2020; Paul et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), and may further threaten human health 10

through dietary exposure and food-chain transfer (Prata et al., 2024). MPs have also been detected 11

in tap and bottled water consumed daily, with fibers and fragments reported as dominant shapes (Al- 12

Mansoori et al., 2024). Therefore, developing efficient detection technologies for MPs in surface 13

water is essential for understanding their environmental behavior, ecological risks, and potential 14

human exposure pathways. 15

Reliable detection of MPs in real surface-water samples remains challenging. Their small size 16

and diverse physical characteristics often lead to misidentification or underestimation during 17

analysis (Huang et al., 2023). In addition, complex filter-membrane backgrounds, including 18

turbidity, black carbon, and light reflection, can substantially reduce detection accuracy (Buaruk et 19

al., 2024). 20

Traditional quantitative methods mainly include visual inspection, microscopic observation, 21

and fluorescence microscopy (Ivleva, 2021). Visual inspection is generally used for particles larger 22

than 1 mm (Ory et al., 2018), but it is highly subjective and easily affected by nonplastic materials, 23

resulting in frequent misclassification (Lv et al., 2019). Microscopic observation is applicable to 24

particles larger than 100 μm, but it remains time-consuming, labor-intensive, and operator- 25

dependent (Zhao et al., 2025a). These limitations make conventional methods insufficient for rapid, 26

objective, and quantitative MPs analysis in complex surface-water samples. 27

To improve detection efficiency, computer vision combined with machine learning has been 28

proposed for rapid and low-cost quantitative analysis of MPs in environmental samples (Guo et al., 29


<!-- Page 6 -->


4

2024). Current approaches mainly include image classification, instance segmentation, and object 30

detection (Hu et al., 2024). Image classification methods, such as VGG- and CNN-based models 31

(Pensiri et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2021), are effective for identifying isolated or single-category MPs, 32

but they generally lack particle-level localization, counting, and size quantification capabilities in 33

full-field microscopic images (Thammasanya et al., 2024). Instance segmentation methods, 34

including U-Net and Mask R-CNN (Cao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2024), can delineate target 35

boundaries, but they often require large annotated datasets and substantial computational resources 36

(Kaur et al., 2024). By contrast, object detection methods require fewer computational resources 37

(Ding et al., 2025), provide faster inference speed (Chen et al., 2024), and support simultaneous 38

detection of multiple MPs categories (Liang et al., 2024). Representative object detection models 39

include R-CNN, YOLO, and DETR (Redmon et al., 2016). Among them, YOLO-based detectors 40

have shown advantages over Mask R-CNN and RT-DETR in detection speed, accuracy, and resource 41

consumption, as summarized in the Supporting Information (SI), specifically in Text S1 and Table 42

S1 (Galata et al., 2024; Jun et al., 2024). Therefore, YOLO-based object detection is technically 43

suitable for high-throughput automated MPs analysis. 44

However, these model-level advantages do not fully address the sample-specific challenges of 45

MPs detection in real surface-water micrographs. Most existing object detection studies have 46

directly transferred general-purpose architectures to MPs detection, with limited adaptation to the 47

intrinsic physical and imaging characteristics of MPs in environmental water samples. MPs often 48

appear as small, low-contrast, and irregularly shaped particles with diverse morphologies, whereas 49

filter-membrane patterns, water stains, inorganic particles, suspended debris, and uneven 50

backgrounds can interfere with model recognition. Consequently, existing models may suffer from 51

missed detection of small or low-contrast MPs, false positives caused by background interference, 52

limited robustness in environmental samples, and insufficient support for particle size quantification 53

(Wang et al., 2023). Therefore, current methods are limited not only by detection accuracy, but also 54

by the lack of model optimization specifically tailored to MPs detection, particularly for small- 55

object perception, background-interference suppression, morphology-aware recognition, and 56

quantitative particle analysis. 57

To overcome these limitations, we propose YOLO-MPs, an improved YOLO11-based 58


<!-- Page 7 -->


5

architecture for rapid and accurate detection of five morphologies of MPs in surface water. By 59

introducing a spatial-channel reconstruction mechanism, YOLO-MPs enhances fine-particle feature 60

representation and improves the detection of small and low-contrast MPs. A dual-attention 61

mechanism was further introduced to strengthen the model’s focus on discriminative regions of MPs 62

and suppress interference from complex microscopic backgrounds. These mechanisms enable 63

simultaneous localization, counting, morphological classification, and micron-level size 64

quantification of fibers, fragments, films, pellets, and linear particles. In addition, a pixel-to-physical 65

size mapping strategy was developed to extend the framework from object detection to quantitative 66

analysis of MPs, providing an efficient and reliable tool for MPs pollution monitoring in real 67

surface-water samples. 68

2. Data and Methods 69

2.1. Dataset Acquisition, Processing, and Annotation 70

2.1.1 Sample Preparation 71

Water samples were collected from the Xiasha section of the Qiantang River, Hangzhou, in 72

September 2024. A 0.45 μm filter membrane (Shanghai Xingya Purification Material Factory) was 73

used to filter 10 L of water sample. Solid impurities on the membrane were transferred to a 500mL 74

glass beaker. MPs were separated using saturated NaCl solution density flotation (Enenche et al., 75

2024). First, 300mL of saturated NaCl solution was added to the solid impurities, thoroughly mixed, 76

and ultrasonicated for 2 minutes, followed by magnetic stirring for 30 minutes, and then settling for 77

24 hours. After settling, the supernatant was placed in a 500mL conical flask. The above steps were 78

repeated three times to obtain a supernatant collection. The collected supernatant was filtered using 79

a vacuum filtration device, selecting a 0.45μm mixed cellulose grid filter membrane (diameter 3mm). 80

The gridded membrane design facilitated zoned observation, ensuring complete imaging of all 81

membrane regions (Tamiya et al., 2024). To digest organic matter on the membrane, 30% H₂O₂ was 82

added dropwise using a rubber-tipped dropper (Zhao et al., 2025b), and left at room temperature for 83

24h. Finally, the membrane was placed in a glass Petri dish with the solid impurity-accumulated 84

side facing upwards for analysis. To avoid external environmental MPs contamination (detailed 85

information of QA/QC shown in Text S1, SI), all containers in the experimental steps were washed 86

with deionized water and sealed with aluminum foil. 87


<!-- Page 8 -->


6

Subsequently, to establish a reliable ground truth and eliminate false positives, representative 88

particles from the five morphological categories were validated using an Infrared-Raman combined 89

microscope analysis system (AIRsight, Shimadzu, Japan). Only chemically confirmed synthetic 90

polymers were retained for bounding box annotations, ensuring the absolute fidelity of the YOLO- 91

MPs training dataset. 92

2.1.2 Training Dataset Image Acquisition 93

This study selected the NE700 upright biological microscope (40 million pixels) for systematic 94

sample observation. Using a 5x objective lens (numerical aperture 0.12) optical configuration, it 95

enabled clear identification of MPs particles >1μm in size. To ensure full sample coverage, a gridded 96

scanning strategy was implemented through precise stage displacement control. Each 3mm gridded 97

membrane underwent 170 positioning shots along the horizontal axis, cumulatively acquiring 98

approximately 170 high-resolution images (4096 x 3112 pixels) to form a complete spatial sampling 99

sequence. Original images were stored in TIFF format, preserving optical signal intensity gradient 100

information but resulting in a single dataset size of 60-70MB. Format conversion code was used to 101

batch-convert images to JPEG format with a compression quality factor of 85%. This processing- 102

maintained image texture feature identifiability (SSIM>0.95) while optimizing total storage 103

requirements to 5-7 MB, a reduction of over 90%. Finally, a raw dataset of 1013 JPEG-format MPs- 104

in-water images was obtained. 105

2.1.3 Model Dataset Preprocessing 106

To enhance the performance and robustness of the MPs image classification model, we 107

implemented a targeted preprocessing pipeline for the original dataset. First, to ensure label 108

accuracy and reliability, we implemented data cleaning, including: meticulous image screening— 109

eliminating blurry and interfering samples; and detailed label correction—fixing all erroneous labels 110

that could lead to misjudgment. This series of measures aimed to significantly enhance the model's 111

recognition accuracy across all categories. Second, to address the issue of uneven sample 112

distribution in the dataset, we implemented a sample balancing strategy. On one hand, redundant 113

data was streamlined—removing photos with excessive fragment-type samples; on the other hand, 114

data was proactively expanded—strengthening sample collection for other underrepresented 115

categories. This process ultimately formed a core dataset of 600 high-quality images with balanced 116


<!-- Page 9 -->


7

class distribution, ensuring the model could learn features of all categories fairly during training. 117

Finally, to further enhance the model's adaptability (generalization ability) in real-world complex 118

scenarios and increase dataset diversity and richness, we creatively applied various data 119

augmentation techniques based on the optimized 600-image core dataset (Pensiri et al., 2024). 120

Simulating various conditions in real MPs microscopic examination include: 1) Horizontal and 121

vertical flipping to simulate appearance changes from different viewing angles; 2) Random 122

brightness adjustment to simulate the impact of lighting changes in microscopic environments on 123

image features; 3) Adding salt-and-pepper noise to simulate potential occluding particle interference 124

during sample filtration. By implementing these three enhancement methods, we effectively 125

expanded the core dataset into a more robust and generalizable 3000-image dataset (600 core images 126

+ 2400 augmented images), providing a more comprehensive perspective and ability to handle 127

complex situations for model learning. 128

2.1.4 Annotation 129

During the annotation phase, LabelImg software was used to classify MPs based on their 130

morphological features. LabelImg is an open-source image annotation tool, and its labels can be 131

used for classification and object detection (Hao et al., 2024). MPs were annotated into five 132

categories based on physical morphology: Linear: Typically refers to thick lines, where length is 133

significantly greater than width (length-to-width ratio >5), commonly from broken textiles or 134

fishing nets (Figure 1(A)).Fragment: Irregularly shaped solid fragments, usually with edges and 135

sharp corners, primarily originating from weathering and mechanical abrasion of larger plastic 136

products, such as packaging materials, plastic bottles, etc. (Figure 1(B)). Fiber: Similar to linear 137

MPs, these are elongated, filamentous MPs, usually softer, commonly from shedding of clothing 138

fibers like polyester (Figure 1(C)). Pellet: Regularly shaped round or cylindrical hard particles, 139

classified as primary MPs, raw materials for plastic product production (nurdles), also commonly 140

used as scrubbing ingredients in cosmetics and beauty products (Figure 1(D)). Film: Flake-shaped 141

MPs, soft and thin with irregular edges, typically originating from the fragmentation of plastic 142

packaging bags, food wrappers, or agricultural plastic films (Figure 1(E)). Precise annotation of 143

these five MPs morphotypes provided high-quality label information for subsequent model training. 144

2.1.5 Data Partition 148

This study employed the hold-out method for dataset partitioning, randomly dividing the 149

dataset into three mutually exclusive sets: training set (70%), validation set (10%), and test set (20%). 150

This partitioning ensures the training set can fully learn data features, the validation set is used for 151

model tuning during iterations, and the test set is used for final performance evaluation, providing 152

a reasonable data distribution for model training and assessment (Pérez-Porras et al., 2022). 153

2.2. Model Construction and Training 154

2.2.1 YOLO-MPs Model Construction 155

Based on the challenges posed by the small size, multi-scale presence, and complex 156

backgrounds of MPs in surface water, this study introduces two key enhancements to the 157

YOLOv11n architecture (the baseline model is detailed in Text S2, SI). These improvements aim 158

to optimize feature extraction and focus mechanisms: a feature reconstruction convolution based on 159

Spatial and Channel Reconstruction Convolution (SCConv) and a deformable attention mechanism 160

(DAM) (Fig. S1). The corresponding theoretical formulations of these modifications are provided 161

in Text S3 and S4, respectively (SI). 162

It is imperative to note that the integration of the SCConv and the DAM into the YOLO11-n 163

framework is not merely a heuristic combination of existing modules. Rather, it is a targeted 164

architectural design fundamentally driven by the unique physical, optical, and morphological 165

characteristics of MPs in environmental samples. 166

First, from an optical perspective, MPs in surface water typically present as small, semi- 167

transparent targets with low optical contrast against complex backgrounds (e.g., filter grids, water 168

stains, and residual organic matter). Standard convolutions process such microscopic images with 169

high spatial redundancy, inevitably dedicating significant computational resources to uniform 170


<!-- Page 11 -->


9

background noise rather than the target itself. SCConv directly addresses this physical challenge. 171

By mathematically suppressing spatial redundancy and reweighting channel features, SCConv 172

forces the network to concentrate on the salient, fine-grained optical variations of the MPs, perfectly 173

aligning with the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio of MPs microscopic imaging. 174

Second, ranging from highly curled fibers to jagged irregular fragments, MPs exhibit an 175

extreme morphological diversity that creates a fundamental mismatch with the rigid, square 176

receptive fields of conventional convolutional neural networks from a geometric perspective. When 177

processing irregular topological shapes, fixed-grid convolutions inevitably sample a substantial 178

amount of irrelevant background pixels. DAM overcomes this spatial constraint by introducing 179

learnable 2D offsets. This mechanism allows the network's receptive field to dynamically deform 180

and seamlessly trace the actual physical contours of the MPs. 181

Synergistically, SCConv ensures that the faint optical signals of small MPs are effectively 182

amplified and distinguished from the background, while DAM guarantees that the feature extraction 183

geometrically strictly follows the irregular boundaries of the particles. Together, this integrated 184

architecture addresses the weak optical signatures and diverse morphologies of MPs in aquatic 185

environments, improving detection under complex microscopic backgrounds. 186

2.2.2 Selection of Training Strategies 187

The parameters of training strategy for the YOLO-MPs model are presented in Table S2 (SI). 188

he input image size was set to 640x640, training epochs to 450, batch size to 32, and 4 data loading 189

threads (workers) were configured to ensure efficiency in data preprocessing and training. The SGD 190

(Stochastic Gradient Descent) optimizer was selected in this study. 191

2.2.3 Model Validation and Evaluation 192

To comprehensively evaluate the model's generalization performance, not only a scientific 193

experimental estimation method is needed but also clear evaluation criteria are required to measure 194

generalization ability. This study adopted the following four metrics for performance assessment: 195

Precision, Recall, mAP@0.5, and mAP@0.5:0.95. These metrics comprehensively reflect the 196

model's performance in practical applications from different dimensions, providing important basis 197

for model optimization and improvement (Cheng et al., 2025). 198

In machine learning classification tasks, Precision (P) and Recall (R) are crucial metrics for 199

2.2.4 Model Deployment and Size-Detection Module 231

To validate the model's practical application effect in environmental water samples, we 232

designed a comparative experiment, comparing YOLO-n (official open-source version), YOLO- 233

MPs (optimized version), and human visual recognition. In the experiment, we used 100 MPs 234

images from test dataset to ensure data representativeness and consistency. This study also 235

developed an automated module for physical dimension measurement. This module calibrates key 236

microscope imaging parameters (e.g., objective magnification and camera pixel size) to calculate 237

the system's effective magnification, thereby establishing a pixel-to-micron conversion coefficient. 238

Ultimately, the system utilizes the pixel dimensions of the detection bounding boxes and this 239

conversion coefficient to achieve automatic micron-level measurement of targets, forming a closed- 240

loop "detection-localization-measurement" process. 241

2.2.5 Practical Application in the Qiantang River 242

In June 2025, water samples were collected from six representative sites within the core water 243

supply area of the Qiantang River (Fig.S2). This sampling aimed to rigorously validate the practical 244

performance of the YOLO-MPs model through a scientifically stringent methodology. 245

After completing the pretreatment steps of vacuum filtration, density flotation, and digestion 246

for the water samples, the entire filter membrane is photographed under a microscope, yielding 247

approximately 170 images per membrane. The YOLO-MPs model was then employed to conduct 248

object detection on the image data from all six sampling sites, with a confidence threshold set to 0.4 249

to prioritize recall rate. The model autonomously output quantitative data on MPs abundance, 250

morphological classifications, and physical dimensions for each site. 251

3. Results and discussion 252


<!-- Page 14 -->


12

3.1. Dataset Optimization 253

In object detection model training, dataset quality is a key factor affecting model generalization 254

ability. The current study first quantitatively evaluated the annotation distribution of the MPs dataset. 255

Spatial distribution analysis showed that target bounding boxes exhibited uniform dispersion 256

characteristics within the images (Fig. S3(A)), with no spatial clustering observed. Bounding box 257

size analysis revealed that approximately 73% of targets had normalized dimensions (width x height 258

product) concentrated in the 0-0.01 interval (Fig.S3(B)), indicating that small-scale targets 259

dominated the dataset. This small-target-dominated data distribution significantly increases 260

detection difficulty, particularly prone to insufficient feature extraction and localization deviation. 261

Furthermore, systematic analysis of the original MPs dataset identified two core challenges: 1) 262

Severe sample imbalance: As shown in Fig.S4(A), Fragment class samples exceeded 8000 instances, 263

while Film, Fiber, and other three classes each had fewer than 2000 samples. This imbalance stems 264

from natural morphological distribution differences of MPs in surface water, causing the model to 265

overfit the dominant class; 2) Label noise and misclassification: The normalized confusion matrix 266

(Fig.S5) showed that the Film class classification accuracy was significantly lower than other 267

classes, and Background samples were frequently misclassified as Fragment, indicating issues with 268

ambiguous labeling or unclear boundary definitions. 269

Our study adopted a two-stage optimization scheme to address these challenges: 1) Data 270

cleaning: Removal of images with blurry targets (12% of total) and re-annotation of Film class 271

bounding boxes, correcting semantic overlap areas between Fragment and Background; 2) Sample 272

balancing: Stratified random discarding applied to the Fragment class (reducing samples by 50%), 273

and GAN-based sample synthesis implemented for underrepresented classes (Film, Pellet, Fiber, 274

Linear classes supplemented by 20% samples). 275

The optimized dataset showed significant improvement: Class distribution standard deviation 276

decreased from original σ=0.31 to σ=0.18 (Fig. S4(B)), Film class classification accuracy increased 277

by 75%, and the misclassification rate for background categories dropped from 23% to 8%. The 278

model performance was improved using the same YOLO framework for training, the accuracy 279

increased from 66.08% to 90.21% (Δ+24.13%), confirming the critical role of data quality 280

optimization for performance. 281

3.2. Model Structure Optimization Strategy 282

Targeting core challenges in the dataset such as small-scale target dominance, multi-scale 283

interference, and complex background noise, the current study systematically implemented a dual- 284

path improvement strategy based on the YOLO11-n model: attention mechanism optimization and 285

feature extraction enhancement. To quantitatively evaluate the independent contributions and 286

synergistic effects of each module, ablation experiments were conducted under strictly consistent 287

training epochs (epochs=300) and hyperparameters. Experimental results are shown in Table 1. The 288

baseline performance of the original YOLO11-n model was 81.66% mAP@0.5. 289

In microscopic images of environmental water samples, MPs are often accompanied by 290

complex background interference, such as water stains and residual organic matter, which can 291

distract model attention and compromise the stable identification of MPs targets. Although the 292

C2PSA module in the YOLO11-n model enhances responses to key regions by integrating attention 293

mechanisms with the CSP structure, its ability to comprehensively capture spatial information in 294

complex environmental scenes remains limited (Xia et al., 2022). To address this issue, a DAM was 295

introduced. By learning adaptive offsets to dynamically adjust attention positions, DAM enables the 296

model to focus on informative MPs regions. While maintaining the fundamental Query–Key–Value 297

computation of self-attention, DAM allows the spatial positions of Keys and Values to adapt to the 298

content of environmental images, thereby facilitating flexible attention to relevant target regions 299

(Figure 2 & Fig.S6). Furthermore, the output features of DAM were fused with those from the 300

C2PSA module to exploit their complementary strengths in spatial information representation and 301

feature characterization, enhancing the discriminability and stability of MPs features and improving 302

detection reliability in complex environmental samples. As a result, DAM enhances perceptual 303

robustness under complex backgrounds by dynamically adjusting the receptive field, improving 304

detection accuracy to 82.50% (Δ+0.84%). The enhanced model detects MPs of varied sizes, shapes, 305

and occlusion levels more accurately, effectively reducing missed and false detections in complex 306

scenarios. 307

*Figure 2. Deformable attention mechanism used in YOLO-MPs 309*

Given that MPs particles in environmental microscopic images predominantly exhibit small 310

sizes and pronounced scale variability, conventional feature extraction strategies often fail to 311

adequately represent their spatial structures and discriminative characteristics. To enhance the 312

detection of small MPs targets in environmental samples, the SCConv feature reconstruction 313

convolution was integrated into the feature extraction backbone of the YOLO11-n model. SCConv 314

improves small-object representation through joint reconstruction of spatial and channel features. 315

Specifically, the Spatial Reconstruction Unit (SRU) refines spatial feature representations to 316

enhance the localization and detection of small MPs targets, while the Channel Reconstruction Unit 317

(CRU) reweights feature channels to strengthen discriminative fine-grained features of MPs 318

particles (Fig.S7&S8). Through these targeted enhancements, the model achieves improved 319

representation of MPs across different scales, providing more reliable detection and quantitative 320

analysis in complex environmental samples. 321

The integration of SCConv significantly mitigates background misclassification, while the 322

DAM module dynamically focuses on critical irregular regions. Combining these modules in the 323

final YOLO-MPs model yielded a synergistic performance leap through an "attention-guided feature 324

reconstruction" mechanism. As demonstrated by the ablation results (Table 1) and the PR curves 325

(Figure 3), the optimized YOLO-MPs model achieved consistent performance gains across all MPs 326

categories, reaching a remarkable overall mAP@0.5 of 92.68% (significantly outperforming the 327

baseline YOLOv11-n model's 90.21%). 328

0.900, and for linear from 0.914 to 0.958. Furthermore, the model attained an overall precision of 332

93.01%, demonstrating a high rate of correct detections with low false positives, and a recall of 333

85.26%, indicating a strong capability to identify the majority of actual MPs targets. These results 334

collectively indicate that the proposed optimization strategy effectively enhanced the accuracy and 335

reliability of morphology-resolved MPs recognition. 336

From a mechanistic perspective, SCConv strengthens the discriminative representation of 337

small-sized MPs through joint reconstruction of spatial and channel features, thereby improving the 338

recognition stability of discrete particle types such as Fragments and Pellets. In contrast, DAT 339

enables adaptive focusing on MPs regions under complex environmental backgrounds, exhibiting 340

superior feature capture capability for morphologies characterized by irregular shapes, elongated 341

structures, or deformation, including Film, Fiber, and Linear MPs. The synergistic integration of 342

SCConv and DAT significantly enhances the model’s comprehensive perception of diverse MPs 343

morphologies, thereby improving the accuracy and reliability of morphology-resolved MPs 344

detection in environmental samples. 345

3.4. Application of human-machine detection comparison 366

Traditional MPs detection consists of a series of time-consuming, resource-intensive, and error- 367

prone procedures. This study introduced YOLO, an object detection technology to replace the 368

quantitative analysis component of traditional visual inspection. Specifically, we used an 369

independent set of 100 un-trained dataset images for annotation and detection. The annotation 370

results serve as the true value for evaluating the detection performance of both the YOLO model 371

and human vision. During deployment, YOLO-MPs detection accuracy was strictly evaluated 372

against µFTIR identification. Cross-validation between the model's visual predictions and the 373

µFTIR chemical spectra confirmed a robust matching rate, demonstrating the model's capability to 374

accurately distinguish true MPs from complex aquatic backgrounds. The YOLO11-n and YOLO- 375

MPs models were employed for detection, and detection accuracy, processing time, and the number 376

of each MPs type detected were recorded in detail. Additionally, three professionally trained 377

experimenters performed manual visual inspection on the same set of images, recording their 378

detection accuracy, time, and quantities for each MPs type, enabling comparative analysis with 379

machine detection results. 380

In the comparative experiment, the YOLO algorithm demonstrated significant superiority over 381

human visual detection. YOLO-MPs achieved the highest accuracy in most categories, particularly 382

excelling in Fragment and Pellet detection, with accuracies of 99.1% and 97.5% respectively— 383

significantly higher than human detection (74.8% and 60.5%) (Figure 4). YOLO-MPs exhibited 384

remarkable advantages in MPs target detection tasks. With an average processing time of 1.28 385

seconds per image (≈ 47 images/min), it was 13.03 times faster than manual detection (3.34 minutes 386

per image) (Fig.S10(A)). YOLO-MPs achieved a detection rate of 94.8%, closest to the ground truth, 387

while the human group suffered over 24.3% missed detection due to visual fatigue (Fig.S10(B)). 388

Additionally, cross-verification by three experimental technicians revealed that water stains are 389

frequently misidentified as fibers, while particulate matter is often confused with debris. 390

Furthermore, experimenters required rest after each batch of 100 images before proceeding. The 391

experiment demonstrated that the structurally optimized YOLO-MPs can replace manual labor for 392

automated, high-throughput quantitative MPs analysis. 393

3.5. Size detection of MPs 396

Based on the YOLO-MPs detection results, this study developed an automated module for 397

measuring the physical dimensions of MPs in surface-water micrographs. By establishing a pixel- 398

to-physical scale conversion, the module automatically converts the bounding-box coordinates 399

generated by YOLO-MPs into micrometer-scale width, height, and area measurements, with the 400

detailed derivation provided in Text S5 (SI). The measurement results show that YOLO-MPs can 401

quantify MPs from the tens-of-micrometers scale to the millimeter scale. Notably, the smallest 402

detected particle in the analyzed dataset reached approximately 40.32×46.08 μm. This result 403

indicates that the proposed model can support tens-of-micrometers-scale detection and size 404

quantification in real surface-water micrographs. Together, the detection results and size 405

measurement module establish an integrated “detection–localization–measurement” workflow, and 406

validation using a standard calibration micro-ruler further confirmed the reliability of the automated 407

size measurements (Figs. S11 and S12). 408

4. Conclusions 450

In this study, we developed YOLO-MPs, an improved YOLO11-based model for rapid 451

detection and quantitative analysis of MPs in surface-water samples. To address the challenges of 452

low optical contrast, small particle size, diverse morphologies, and complex microscopic 453

backgrounds in microscopic monitoring images, a spatial-channel reconstruction mechanism and a 454

dual-attention mechanism were introduced into the YOLO11-n framework. The spatial-channel 455

reconstruction mechanism enhanced fine-particle feature representation, while the dual-attention 456


<!-- Page 23 -->


21

mechanism strengthened the model’s focus on discriminative regions of MPs and suppressed 457

background interference. This design improved the detection of five representative morphologies of 458

MPs, including films, fragments, pellets, fibers, and linear particles, especially for irregular, slender, 459

or deformed particles that are difficult to identify under complex microscopic conditions. YOLO- 460

MPs achieved 93.01% precision and 92.68% mAP@0.5, with an inference time of 1.28 s per image, 461

and the overall detection process was 13.03-fold faster than manual visual inspection. 462

In addition to morphology-based detection, an automated physical-dimension measurement 463

module was developed based on the proportional relationship between actual size and pixel scale. 464

By integrating this module, YOLO-MPs enabled simultaneous localization, counting, morphology 465

classification, and micron-level size quantification of MPs. The model was further applied to real 466

surface-water samples from six sampling sites in the core water supply area of the Qiantang River, 467

generating quantitative monitoring data on MPs abundance, morphology composition, and size 468

distribution. These results indicate that YOLO-MPs provides an efficient and automated analytical 469

tool for MPs monitoring and assessment in surface-water environments, supporting image-based 470

data acquisition and quantitative interpretation of MPs pollution patterns in natural waters. Overall, 471

the improved morphology-resolved detection and size-quantification capability strengthens the 472

reliability of MPs characterization and provides technical and quantitative support for surface-water 473

pollution monitoring and environmental assessment. 474

Despite its advantages in detection accuracy and processing efficiency, YOLO-MPs still has 475

limitations. In particular, its detection performance may decrease when the number of MPs in a 476

single image exceeds 20, likely due to object overlap, high target density, and increased background 477

complexity. Therefore, in practical applications, particle density should be appropriately controlled 478

during sample pretreatment, filtration, and image acquisition to improve detection reliability. Future 479

work should further expand the dataset across different water bodies, particle densities, imaging 480

conditions, and MPs aging states to enhance the robustness and generalizability of the model for 481

real-world surface-water monitoring. 482
